Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.

- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
### A Place to Put the River

The first thing we did after buying the house was paint over the line where the river had been.

It ran through the kitchen at the height of my hip, a faint brown seam interrupted by the stove. The previous owner, Mrs. Vale, had pointed it out during the inspection. She stood in the middle of the kitchen with her handbag hanging from both hands.

“That was a Tuesday,” she said.

The inspector asked what year.

“Oh, 1986. But Tuesday was the important part. I’d just washed the floors.”

On our first morning in the house, my brother and I opened a can of pale yellow paint. We were thirty and thirty-four, old enough to know that buying a house together was a questionable solution to several unrelated problems. His marriage had ended. My landlord had decided to sell. There was only one bathroom, and the stairs began directly behind the front door, so that if you came in too enthusiastically you could find yourself in the middle of going upstairs.

We painted the kitchen yellow because the hardware store had mixed five gallons for somebody who never came back.

By lunchtime the river was gone.

In September, my brother found a canoe in the garage. We had been parking beside it for three months without noticing. It hung from the rafters, upside down, its green hull almost black with dust. We got it down with considerable planning and no grace. Inside were two paddles, a wasp nest, and an envelope containing a photograph of Mrs. Vale standing knee-deep in water in our kitchen.

She was wearing a blue robe and holding a colander.

On the back someone had written: *Jean retrieving the potatoes.*

I put the photograph on the refrigerator. My brother took it down because the magnet was scratching the door. I put it back with a different magnet. This was more or less how we had been making decisions since childhood.

Neither of us wanted to go out in the canoe. We wanted to be the kind of people who went out in a canoe, which was different enough to keep it in the garage all winter.

In February a letter came for Mrs. Vale. It was from the hearing clinic and had *PERSONAL* stamped on the front in red. I called the number she had left us. She’d moved into an apartment across from the library, and I offered to bring the letter over.

“Would you?” she said. “I’ve been ignoring their calls for a week.”

Her apartment was hot and smelled of toast. On the windowsill was a row of stones, each with a date written on it in pencil. While she went to find the kettle, I leaned over to read them. Most were from the previous summer. One was dated April 9, 1991.

“I pick one up when I go for a walk,” Mrs. Vale said behind me. “Then I come home and put it down. There’s not a lot to it.”

I asked about the photograph.

“Oh,” she said, “he thought that was terribly funny.”

“Mr. Vale?”

“No, the man from the gas company.”

She told me the river had come in through the back door, which she’d opened to see how high it was. She could still shut the door, but by then there wasn’t much point. The potatoes floated out of a basket under the sink. She had been determined to catch them, because it was something she could see to do.

“What did you do with them?” I asked.

“Threw them away, of course.”

In March it rained for six days. My brother went down to the river each evening and returned with a report that meant nothing to me.

“It’s up to the bench.”

“Which bench?”

“The one you can’t see anymore.”

On the seventh morning, we woke to a woman knocking on the door. She lived two streets over and had been knocking on doors since five. The river had come into her yard. She recommended moving the cars uphill while we could. My brother started looking for his keys, and the woman, who could see them on the hall table from where she stood, reached in and handed them to him.

The water didn’t reach our house. It reached the end of the driveway and stayed there for half a day. All that time our cars sat at the top of the hill with the other cars, and people walked down in twos and threes to look at their houses. A man carried a toaster uphill under his arm. Nobody asked him why he had chosen the toaster.

Late that afternoon my brother and I took the canoe off its hooks. We set it on the driveway and sat in it, facing the river. Our feet were dry. The paddles lay across our knees.

“Do you know how to steer this?” he asked.

“No.”

“Good,” he said, and took his feet out of his wet shoes.

We sat there until the woman who’d knocked on our door came back down the street. She looked at us for a moment, then asked if there was room for one more. My brother moved forward. She climbed in, carefully, with a hand on each of our shoulders. She had been on her feet since before dawn.

The next time I visited Mrs. Vale, she wanted to know how close the water had gotten. I said I’d show her, and the following Saturday she came over. We stood at the mouth of the driveway. In the gravel there was a ragged line of leaves and little sticks, with a blue plastic clothespin caught among them.

From there I could see straight through the kitchen window to the yellow wall. I asked if she remembered exactly where the old line had been.

She came inside and considered the wall for a while. Then she put one finger against it, just below a light switch.

“Here,” she said. After a second she moved her finger down. “No. Here.”

I offered to get a pencil.

Mrs. Vale thought about it. “Have you still got that photograph?”

I showed her where it was on the refrigerator. She straightened it, although I hadn’t noticed it was crooked. Then she asked if we had any coffee, and I put the kettle on.
---

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION. A quietly comic, carefully structured short story uses a flood, a family home, and its objects to explore how people live alongside loss and change.

## Grounded reading
The voice is measured and observant, finding humor in practical details without making light of the characters’ vulnerability. The brother and narrator’s shared house is a makeshift answer to separate disruptions; their awkward, matter-of-fact closeness gradually opens to include Mrs. Vale and a neighbor. The story’s pathos rests less on catastrophe than on the small acts people can manage within it: catching potatoes, moving cars, sitting in a canoe, making coffee. Its ending invites the reader to accept an imperfect record of the past—the finger that changes position on the wall—and to value the companionship that remains.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds floodwater and its traces: the painted-over waterline, the photograph, stones dated in pencil, and leaves and sticks left in the driveway. It pairs these with humble objects and tasks—the canoe, potatoes, toaster, kettle—to make people’s responses to danger and memory concrete. Its moral emphasis is gentle: care often takes the form of noticing, offering a seat, or staying present rather than finding a grand solution.

## Evidence line
> We wanted to be the kind of people who went out in a canoe, which was different enough to keep it in the garage all winter.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the story’s recurring objects and understated humor make its attention to memory, practical care, and companionship unusually distinctive within the sample.
